held_reason: Second attempt, 2026-11-20. Fixed: the unit is now limited to actuators reached from under the dashboard or behind the glove box, and all four examples have a genuine-part list price (the economy example is now a 2015 Chevrolet Cruze, the truck a 2016 Chevrolet Silverado 1500, the luxury car a 2015 Infiniti Q50). Still missing: a labor time that can honestly be used as a range end. The only figure used is a parts seller's 'less than 60 minutes' for the Silverado, as a top. General Motors bulletins for the Cruze, Malibu, Tahoe and Escalade name the temperature actuator replacement operation but print 'Use Published Labor Operation Time' instead of a figure; Infiniti's Q50 bulletin and Nissan's Titan bulletin print 0.5 and 0.6 with no unit; Ford's times include diagnosis or housing removal; and FCA's 0.6 Hrs 'Test and Replace' was re-read: its test is the calibration test run before the actuator is removed, to decide whether to replace it, not a calibration after fitting, so it does not meet the condition set for using it. No aftermarket price was found on a page that says new for any class; three lows are the discounted genuine part and the truck low is null. Three classes have parts from one seller only.
unit: per job: one HVAC air-mix (blend / temperature) door actuator that can be reached from under the dashboard or behind the glove box, fitted and calibrated. Vehicles where the dashboard or the HVAC housing has to come out to reach the actuator are not covered by this estimate: that is a much larger job. Not included: mode (air distribution) or recirculation (intake) door actuators, a second temperature actuator on dual-zone systems, the HVAC box or the blend door itself, and diagnosis

hours_src.what: Cross-check: the example vehicle and the right door, but the time includes a test that decides whether the actuator is replaced. FCA bulletin 24-005-16 Rev. B (July 2, 2016; 2014-2015 Chrysler Town & Country and Dodge Grand Caravan, 'Blend Door Stuck In Full Heat Mode', X64 warranty extension) states op 24-55-23-90 'Actuator, A/C and Heater Right Temperature Blend Door - Test and Replace' 0.6 Hrs. Re-read on 2026-11-20: the procedure runs the Actuator Calibration Test first, then removes the right instrument panel silencer and checks the linkage, and only then removes and fits the actuator; after fitting it calls for a heating and cooling test, not a calibration. So the 'test' is a before-the-repair check, not a calibration after fitting, and the time is not used as a range end. It is a warranty time, the low end of what a shop bills, and the actuator is reached by removing the silencer panel only. This is the closest thing found to a usable time for this job

finding: New job, so there is no live range to compare, and this file is HELD: it is not complete enough to show. The unit is now limited to actuators that can be reached from under the dashboard or behind the glove box; vehicles where the dashboard or HVAC housing has to come out are not covered (Ford's F-150 bulletin prints 5.0 to 5.6 Hrs for that, Lexus 6.5 with no unit). Parts are now priced for all four examples from the genuine part: economy 2015 Chevrolet Cruze $76.84-$158.58, midsize 2015 Chrysler Town & Country $95.46-$144.00, truck 2016 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 up to $84.33, luxury 2015 Infiniti Q50 $78.55-$113.83. In three classes the low is the same genuine part at a dealer-parts seller's discount, not an aftermarket price, and the truck has no low: aftermarket actuators are listed for the Silverado at about $24-$41 and for the minivan at about $16-$26, but none of those pages says the part is new, so they are cross-checks only. Labor is still the gap. No maker time was found that can honestly be used for this unit. General Motors bulletins name exactly this operation ('Temperature Valve Actuator Replacement') for the Cruze, Malibu, Tahoe and Escalade but print 'Use Published Labor Operation Time' instead of a figure. FCA's warranty bulletin for the minivan prints 0.6 Hrs to 'Test and Replace' the right temperature blend door actuator; on re-reading, the test is the calibration test run before the actuator is taken out, to decide whether it is replaced, so it is a check before the repair and not a calibration after fitting, and it stays a cross-check. Infiniti's Q50 bulletin prints 0.5 and Nissan's Titan bulletin 0.6 for replacing an air mix door motor, both with no unit; the Q50 bulletin says plainly that neither the instrument panel nor the heater case is removed. Ford's Fiesta bulletin prints 1.0 Hrs, but for the air distribution actuator and including diagnosis. The only figure used is a top for the truck: a parts seller's listing says most owners can replace the Silverado's temperature actuator 'in less than 60 minutes', taken as 1 hour; it is a seller's statement for an owner at home, not a book time. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks) can therefore only be given for the truck top: up to about $244 ($84.33 plus 1 hour at $160). For illustration only, not a published range: if the unitless and test-included maker figures of 0.5 to 0.6 are read as hours, the four examples would come to roughly $137-$255, which is below every benchmark (FIXD $308-$355; RepairPal model pages from $138-$166 up to $1,149-$1,588). The benchmarks' very wide spread matches the bulletins: cheap where the actuator is reachable, $900 and up where the dash or HVAC unit comes out, and several benchmark figures clearly include that larger job, which this unit now excludes. To finish: load a labor-guide figure for the GM temperature valve actuator operation or another maker time with a unit for a bare replacement in each class, and find an aftermarket actuator for each example on a page that says new and names the year. Confidence is low: no class has a usable stated labor range and three classes have one parts seller. This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds: diagnosis (scan for HVAC codes, actuator calibration test) since clicking or wrong-temperature air can also be a broken blend door, a binding door, a control head or a software fault; an HVAC control module software update; the second temperature actuator on dual-zone systems, or mode and recirculation actuators found worn at the same time; shop supplies and sales tax. If the actuator cannot be reached without removing the dashboard or HVAC housing, this estimate does not apply: expect many more labor hours and, on some vehicles, an air-conditioning evacuate and recharge and coolant top-up.
